h1: Corn, rye, wheat and rice: how the grain shapes a whisky
title: Corn, Rye, Wheat and Rice in Whisky | Craft Beer School
desc: How corn, rye, wheat, rice and malted barley each shape the flavour of a whisky, from sweet bourbon to spicy rye and soft wheated styles.
teaser: Bourbon tastes sweet, rye tastes spicy and wheated whisky feels soft. The grain bill explains most of it.
standfirst: Every whisky starts as a grain. Which grain you use and how much of it set the flavour long before the cask gets its turn.
sections: Why the grain still matters after distillation

Distillation strips out a lot, but not everything. Flavour compounds formed in fermentation, plus traces of the grain itself, carry through into the new make. Pot stills keep more of that character. Column stills run to higher strength and keep less, which is why grain whisky from a column tastes lighter.

Our guide to malt, grain and blended whisky explains the category names. Here we look at what each grain brings to the glass.

Almost every whisky contains some malted barley, even when it is not the main grain. Malting develops enzymes that turn starch into fermentable sugar during the mash. Corn, rye and unmalted wheat have very little enzyme power of their own, so a portion of malt does the conversion for the whole mash, sometimes with added enzymes where rules allow.

When malted barley is the only grain, as in single malt, you get cereal, biscuit, honey and fruity esters from a long fermentation. It is the most expensive grain to use and the most flavourful per litre.

Corn is the backbone of American bourbon, which by US rules must be made from at least 51% corn and aged in new charred oak. Corn gives a sweet, rounded, slightly oily spirit with notes of cornbread and butter. The high starch content also makes it a good yielder.

Corn is cooked at high temperature to gelatinise its starch before the malt enzymes can work on it. A distiller who skimps on the cook gets poor yield and a thin spirit.

Rye brings pepper, clove, mint and a dry, grippy finish. American rye whiskey must be at least 51% rye. Rye is also hard work in the distillery. Its gums make the mash thick and sticky. It can also foam badly in fermentation, so mash tuns, pumps and fermenters need headroom and patience.

Even a 10 to 20% rye share in a corn based bourbon gives a noticeably spicier whisky than a recipe with no rye at all.

Wheat used in place of rye gives a softer, gentler whisky. "Wheated" bourbons swap rye for wheat as the second grain and come across as bready, honeyed and smooth rather than spicy. Wheat is also widely used for grain whisky in Scotland because it yields well in column stills.

Brewers will recognise the same pattern from wheat beers: wheat adds softness and body more than loud flavour.

Rice is less common in whisky but has a long history in Asian spirits. Rice whisky gives a clean, light, slightly floral spirit. In India rice and other grains also feed neutral grain spirit, which is quite different from the molasses spirit used for many local brands. Our guide to molasses versus grain spirit in India sets out that difference.

Some craft distillers experiment with millet, oats or heritage barley. Oats give a creamy texture. Millets are interesting in an Indian context and still largely untested at scale. Anyone trying them should expect to learn the cook, the mash and the yield from scratch.

The grain sets the raw material, but fermentation decides how much of it you keep. Whisky wash is fermented without a boil, often for two to four days. Distillers' yeast throws fruity esters that sit on top of the cereal notes. A short ferment tastes more of grain. A long one tastes more of fruit.

This is why two distilleries using the same corn heavy mash bill can still make whiskies that taste quite different. Mash bill, yeast, fermentation time and still shape stack up. The grain is only the first layer.

Line up a bourbon, a rye whiskey and a single malt, all at similar strength. Nose them with a little water. The bourbon leans sweet and vanilla, partly from new oak. The rye shows pepper and herbs. The malt shows cereal and fruit.

Then ask which part came from the grain and which from the cask. Separating the two takes practice. It is also exactly what distillers do when they design a mash bill.
faqs: Why must bourbon be at least 51% corn?
It is part of the US legal definition of bourbon. The rest of the grain bill can be rye, wheat or malted barley, which changes the character.
Is single malt better than grain whisky?
Not better, different. Single malt is made only from malted barley in pot stills and carries more flavour. Grain whisky is lighter and is the base of most blends.
Can whisky be made from rice?
Yes. Rice whisky exists and tends to be clean and light. Whether it may be called whisky depends on each country's rules.
